Title: MDR Pricing: Comparing Asset-Based and Ingestion-Based Costs
Context: Detection value How does this data support the threats we need to detect
Full Text:
When comparing MDR pricing, it helps to understand what the same annual budget would buy from each provider. Two proposals with similar prices may give analysts access to different evidence, retain it for different periods, or leave your team with different responsibilities. Those differences can affect what happens when you need to investigate a compromised account or trace an attacker’s low-and-slow activity across your environment.

For security leaders weighing asset-based against ingestion-based pricing, a useful comparison starts with the systems you need to protect and the logs required to investigate threats. Giving providers the same requirements and budget helps expose the decisions behind each quote, including what you would need to exclude or pay more to include.

Asset-based vs. ingestion-based MDR pricing

Under asset-based pricing, the charge is tied to a defined population of assets. You need to establish how the provider counts workstations, servers, cloud resources, and other systems, alongside which data sources and service capabilities the price includes. A predictable asset count can help with budgeting, but the proposal still needs to explain any integration limits or additional service charges. At Rapid7, an asset is defined as any physical or virtual endpoint or server running a supported operating system within the monitored environment.

With ingestion-based pricing, some of the cost depends on the volume of data collected or processed. The comparison needs to account for the included allowance, how billable volume is measured, and what happens when usage increases. Retention, search, and supporting infrastructure may also contribute to the overall cost, depending on the commercial model. At Rapid7, MDR customers have access to 13 months hot storage of logs as standard.

Whichever approach you are evaluating, include the technology, analysts, and response support needed to deliver the service. A SIEM ingestion charge on its own cannot be compared directly with an MDR subscription that includes investigation and response. Both proposals need to account for the work your organization expects the provider to perform - this clarity is key to a successful partnership.

How to make a like-for-like MDR pricing comparison

Give each provider the same asset inventory, required data sources, retention needs, and response expectations, then ask what fits within your annual budget. Any exclusions should be visible in the proposal, so you can judge their operational consequences before committing.

For example, one proposal might accommodate endpoint and identity data while requiring you to limit high-volume network sources. Another might accommodate those sources but lack an investigation capability your team needs. Looking at an MDR price per endpoint or per gigabyte will not resolve that difference; you need to see how the service uses the available data.

Use these questions during an initial demonstration to turn the pricing discussion into a practical comparison.

Rapid7 provides 13 months of log retention. Confirm the history available for each data type: 3rd party endpoint alerts have different availability from log-based searches.

Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response, covering investigation, containment, and threat eradication. Incident reports document findings, attacker timelines, and recommended corrective actions.

Asset-based pricing with unlimited ingestion removes data volume as the billing unit. Request a written calculation for additional billable assets and changes to service scope.

What Keyloop’s experience shows about MDR value

For Alan Simpson, now Rapid7’s Field CISO, the ability to collect previously restricted data made a practical difference during his time at Keyloop: "We were previously ingesting around 250 GB a day into Splunk. After moving to Rapid7, we reached 1.4 TB a day, including NetFlow, full DNS logging, and web application firewall logs. These were sources we’d previously had to limit or simply weren’t collecting, so we gained much better visibility and coverage."

The change also extended the history available for investigation, with greater certainty about how long that evidence would remain accessible: "We also moved from around 90 days of retention in Splunk to 13 months with Rapid7. Even those 90 days couldn’t be relied on, as retention depended on how much data we were ingesting at the time. Having a longer, predictable history made a real difference."

Price predictability was key as Keyloop grew through seven mergers and acquisitions, each bringing a different data profile. His experience illustrates why collection and retention belong in the buying decision, although these figures alone do not establish a like-for-like cost saving.

How to compare MDR pricing beyond log volume

Once you understand which data fits within the quote, examine what the provider can do with it. Collecting more logs can close visibility gaps, but useful investigations depend on relevant events, consistent timestamps, and enough context to connect activity to a user or system. AI-assisted investigation also depends on that foundation: a required event that was never recorded leaves an investigation gap.

Infrastructure design can improve the usefulness of that evidence. Routing access to a management interface through a controlled path, for example, creates a clearer monitoring point and helps distinguish expected access from activity requiring investigation. This is why log volume and detection-rule counts need to be assessed alongside how the environment operates.

During a proof of concept, choose a threat scenario relevant to your business and ask the provider to demonstrate the detection, evidence gathering, and response. You should be able to see which records support the conclusion and what happens if a required source is unavailable.

How will your MDR cost change as you grow?

Repeat the comparison using a plausible change, such as an acquisition, additional cloud workloads, or enabling a previously excluded log source. For asset-based pricing, calculate the effect of additional billable assets and changes in scope. For ingestion-based pricing, examine increased daily volume, applicable commitments, and retention requirements. Assuming asset counts stay the same, at Rapid7 contract renewals are capped at 5% uplift, for the contract term, not per year.

Ask both providers to document the assumptions, including implementation effort, required licenses, and work your team will continue to perform. You can then assess what the budget covers today, which evidence remains unavailable, and what it would cost to accommodate the changes you expect.

Full Text:
Microsoft is publishing 1,092 own-product vulnerabilities on November 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Until a few months ago, these volumes would have been unimaginable, but if anything, this month feels like a slight reprieve.

The jury is still out on whether patching many more vulnerabilities will lead to better security outcomes; every code change to resolve a known vulnerability could easily introduce new hidden treasure for researchers or threat actors to unearth in the future.

Despite the vast uptick in volume during 2026, there has been no accompanying increase in the number of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, with no known public disclosure at all this month.

Outlook: zero-day spoofing

Imagine coming home and checking your mailbox to find a postcard. You admire the non-specific image of a tropical beach at sunset, and flip it over to scan the handwriting on the back, which looks vaguely familiar. It’s addressed to you, but you can’t make out the signature, and the message is short and generic. Is that real handwriting, or has this been printed? Probably marketing material.

You put the card in the recycling and, since life is busy, you move on and forget about it. Somehow, you remain entirely unaware that, immediately after reading the postcard, you took out your phone and sent high-resolution images of your front door key to a number you’ve never contacted before.

Is this sketch just some rather questionable science fiction? Yes, hopefully, but what if that non-specific postcard was instead a malicious file in your Outlook inbox? Now we’re talking about CVE-2026-124194, an exploited-in-the-wild spoofing vulnerability. Merely opening a specially crafted malicious file causes Outlook to silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and leak the user’s NTLM v2 hash. All supported versions of classic Outlook receive patches.

The relatively low CVSS v3.1 base score of 6.5 does not tell the full story here, since this vulnerability provides value for both commodity attackers working to harvest initial access at scale, and also more targeted campaigns by more sophisticated threat actors.

The NTLM v2 hash can be relayed live to impersonate the user against another service, at least where those services do not implement adequate safeguards such as message signing for SMB or LDAP, as well as Extended Protection for Authentication for Exchange or Active Directory Certificate Services. Alternatively, the NTLM v2 hash can be cracked offline by a motivated attacker to retrieve the underlying credential. The Preview Pane is not a vector, which will help limit the real-world impact somewhat.

Windows Schannel: critical pre-auth RCE

A pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows will always attract attention. CVE-2026-119952 allows an attacker to execute code on a target system by sending specially crafted malicious packets. Since the vulnerable component is Schannel, which is Microsoft’s implementation of Transport Layer Security (TLS), attackers may not have to look very far to find vulnerable endpoints.

The advisory provides some comfort by pointing out that specific conditions are required for exploitability, which reduces the likelihood of broad exploitation, but the advisory still assesses exploitation as more likely, so Microsoft presumably expects that the development of reliable exploit code is feasible. In many cases, there will be no need for an attacker to have an existing foothold on the same subnet.

The execution context likely depends on the vulnerable service, which points to the evergreen need for least privilege architecture, but it also means that we cannot exclude the possibility of pre-auth RCE as SYSTEM in some cases.

Exchange/Windows Search: critical pre-auth RCE

Could someone take control of your Exchange server by sending a single email? In short: yes. Microsoft offers customers tight integration between various business-critical components. Exchange running on Windows is Microsoft on Microsoft, and the Windows Search component indexes email on behalf of Exchange.

An attacker aiming to exploit CVE-2026-116928 relies on this helpful synergy to achieve pre-auth RCE on the server by sending a malicious attachment, which Exchange will process automatically. How’s that for low attack complexity Although the advisory does not specify the context of execution, we should assume SYSTEM, since several of the services which might be involved do run with a high privilege level.

Since the patches are for Windows OS rather than Exchange itself, there’s no need to worry about which version of Exchange you’re running, so long as you are running only Exchange Subscription Edition, since all previous versions of Exchange are now fully beyond end of support.

Microsoft lifecycle update

There are fewer Microsoft product lifecycle changes in November 2026 than last month. As of Nov 11, 2026, .NET 8 Long Term Servicing channel moves past its release end date, along with PowerShell 7.4 LTS, and the 23H2 versions of the Enterprise, Education, and IoT editions of Windows 11.

Title: Critical vulnerabilities in N-able N-central prompt hosted shutdown
Context: Overview On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and...
Full Text:
Overview

On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details.

As of November 10, N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published PoC code and said it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited. The vendor has advised keeping N-central deployments offline while it develops and validates a hotfix. Hosted N-central classic environments remain offline, according to the same notice. N-able's notice does not yet include CVE identifiers or CVSS scores.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to administer endpoints and infrastructure. Compromise of an RMM server can put downstream managed environments at risk. N-central has previously been targeted through separate vulnerabilities, including an authentication bypass covered by Rapid7 in August 2026. Given the platform's administrative reach and the availability of public exploit code, Rapid7 recommends treating the current disclosure as an emergency.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations operating on-premises N-central servers take them offline immediately and keep them offline until the hotfix is available, and the server has been successfully upgraded. Hosted customers should follow the vendor's service restoration updates. N-able is developing and validating a hotfix, with a target of midday November 10 EST.

Affected versions: The researcher reports testing N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31. N-able's current notice does not specify the full affected-version range.

Fixed versions: N-able's incident notice does not yet identify a remediation build. Follow the incident notice for release confirmation and installation instructions.

Rapid7 also recommends reviewing N-central servers and downstream managed systems for signs of compromise and engaging incident responders if suspicious activity is identified.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to N-able's security incident notice.

Title: Five Signs Your MDR is All Alert, No Action
Context: Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your...
Full Text:
Your managed detection and response (MDR) provider flags suspicious activity, and your analyst spends the next hour finding the account, checking logs, and deciding whether anything needs to happen. By the time the investigation is underway, the alert feels less like help and more like a task assignment.

MDR should bring your team capacity and expertise when it needs them. If the service keeps handing the hardest work back to your analysts, these five signs can help you work out where the arrangement is falling short.

1. Every alert arrives with homework

If your analysts are still sorting through the same recurring false positives, the extra coverage may be creating more work than it removes. Even an alert worth investigating is only so useful when your team has to gather the basic context before it can make a decision. Take a few recent alerts and look at what your provider had already checked when it contacted you. You should be able to see how it separated routine activity from a credible threat, and what it did to stop familiar noise from coming back.

2. It spots the fire, but cannot see the fuel

A suspicious login involving an account with broad access deserves a different response from the same activity on a tightly restricted account. The systems within reach, their importance to the business, and any known weaknesses all help determine what needs attention first. When your MDR leaves your team to assemble that picture during an investigation, valuable time goes into finding context that could have informed the response from the start. Find out how your provider uses information about assets, identities, vulnerabilities, and current threats, including what it can help you address before an incident occurs.

3. Your team gets incident updates, but few useful lessons

When a provider contains a threat and closes the case, your team should come away with more than a record of what happened. Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your environment? If similar activity appears three months later and your analysts have to work through the same questions, the service has missed a chance to make them better prepared. Expertise is most useful when your team can apply some of it next time.

4. Your response support has a spending limit

If an incident is still developing when your included response hours run out, continued specialist support may require another purchasing decision. Limits on hours, incident scope, or responder involvement can turn an agreed service into an unplanned budget request under pressure.

Ask what happens when an investigation expands across systems or continues longer than expected. Establish whether incident response is unlimited, which activities that includes, how long specialists stay involved, and what could trigger additional charges. When business operations and leadership confidence are already at stake, uncertainty about continued support adds financial and operational pressure at the point you need a clear path forward.

5. Your provider’s reports prove it was busy

A monthly report might show hundreds of alerts reviewed and dozens of investigations opened. That gives you a sense of volume, though it says little about what the provider found or did. Choose a closed investigation and follow it from the initial signal through to the outcome: what evidence was considered, what was ruled out, what action was taken, and when did your team become involved? If you need several calls to piece together that story, the charts are doing a better job of showing activity than the service is of showing its work.

If several of these signs feel familiar, bring a few real alerts and investigations to your next service review. Ask your provider to show what it investigated, which actions it took, and what improved afterward. The answers will give you a clearer view of the work your MDR is taking on and the work that still lands with your team.

For more questions to use when reviewing your service, explore the MDR buyer’s guide.

Context: Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path...
Full Text:
Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. The harder problem is deciding which issues create a credible path to business impact, then acting before that path can be used. As frontier AI makes it faster and less expensive to connect weaknesses, operational assumptions, and legitimate system behavior, that decision window is becoming even tighter.

The Gartner® report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, examines what this shift means for cybersecurity priorities and investment. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery.

Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation?

Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path.

The change also extends beyond one model. Gartner states, “By 2027, Mythos will be overtaken by new frontier-AI-enabled models, signaling that this moment is not about Mythos, but a new era of AI-assisted vulnerabilities and functional exploits.”

At Rapid7, we believe this requires a more attacker-aware view of exposure. A large backlog can contain thousands of issues with very different implications for the organization. Leaders need to understand which exposures are reachable, how they could be combined, which business services they affect, and what action would reduce risk most effectively.

What should security leaders measure instead?

Vulnerability counts, backlog size, and generic remediation targets show how much work a team has completed. They provide less clarity on whether an attacker’s options have narrowed or whether the organization can respond and recover more effectively.

Gartner advises, “Organizations must shift focus from volume and activity to speed of decision, effectiveness of response, and tangible reduction of enterprise risk in an environment where attacker reasoning scales rapidly.”

The report examines outcome-driven measures including “Attack path analysis coverage,” “Patching cadence,” “Compensating control deployment cadence,” “Mean time to remediate,” and “Technology debt.” We believe this gives leaders a stronger basis for connecting security investment with reduced exposure, faster action, and business resilience.

How can teams move from prioritization to action?

Better prioritization only creates value when teams can act on it. Gartner recommends, “Use attack path analysis to prioritize your patches, virtual patches, and compensating controls. This can scale down to a consideration of critical services mapped into critical business outcomes and exposure.”

Rapid7’s internal, practitioner-led exploration of Claude Mythos Preview through Project Glasswing reinforces our view that faster discovery is only the beginning. A model may help identify and validate a potential vulnerability, but reducing exposure still requires teams to understand affected systems, apply business context, choose the right remediation or compensating control, verify the result, and maintain detection coverage.

Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path analysis together, helping teams identify which exposures matter most and coordinate remediation through existing workflows.

What does an outcome-led program look like?

An outcome-led program gives executives a clearer answer to a more useful question: which attacker opportunities did we reduce, and how quickly could we respond? It also supports ongoing decisions about technical debt, recovery planning, and where limited resources can deliver the greatest reduction in business risk.

Title: Rapid7 Achieves ISO/IEC 42001 Certification for its AI Management System
Context: Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)
Full Text:
Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider.

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle.

This certification means an accredited third party has audited our AIMS and confirmed that it aligns to the standard. To note, this isn’t a one-time exercise, as the certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits. This means our AI governance program is held to the standard for as long as the certificate is active.

Why is ISO/IEC 42001 certification important?

AI is continually evolving how security teams work, and it’s also causing teams to reconsider the questions they ask their vendors. Where does the model come from? What data does it use? Who reviews its outputs? How do we maintain the integrity and quality of our AI products?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification gives customers independent evidence that Rapid7 has a management system in place to address those questions. It demonstrates that the in-scope AI systems are developed and operated under a structured program covering risk assessment, transparency, human oversight, and accountability.

It also supports customers in their own governance work. Many organizations are building AI risk into their third party risk programs and preparing for frameworks and regulations such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. A vendor's certified AIMS doesn't replace a customer's own due diligence, but it provides a credible, audited starting point.

As with cloud security, AI follows a shared responsibility model. Rapid7 is certified in the role of an AI provider, meaning we’re accountable for how we design, build, and operate these AI systems. Customers remain in control of how they use AI outputs within their own security operations.

Which AI systems are in scope?

The certification covers the AIMS supporting the following AI systems developed within Rapid7 products:

Agentic AI Workflow for MDR (Managed Detection and Response)

AI Dashboard Summary Card (Managed Detection and Response)

AI-Generated Risk Summaries (Exposure Command and Surface Command)

AI-Powered Log Search (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

AI-Powered Log Summary (Incident Command / InsightIDR)

Attack Surface Management (Surface Command)

ICS Runtime Event Story (InsightCloudSec / Cloud Runtime)

Most of these are capabilities customers use directly within the product. Agentic AI Workflow for MDR supports Rapid7's own SOC analysts as they investigate and respond on behalf of MDR customers.

What's next?

ISO/IEC 42001 certification joins Rapid7's existing security and compliance program, which includes ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, IRAP, ENS, BSI C5, as well as U.S. and international cybersecurity regulations. Each is independently assessed against its own defined scope, with details available in the Rapid7 Trust Center (reach out to your Account Executive for access).

As our AI capabilities grow, our AI governance program will grow with them. As such, we'll update this post if the scope of certification changes.

Customers can request a copy of the certificate through their Account Executive or Rapid7 representative. The certificate can also be independently verified in Schellman's public certificate directory.

Title: The Race Against the 3-Day Clock: How Rapid7 Helps Meet BOD 26-04 Compliance
Context: The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were...
Full Text:
Introduction to BOD 26-04

On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached.

The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers.

This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all.

What did CISA actually change?

BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context.

Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't.

The four variables to BOD 26-04

BOD 26-04 abandons CVSS as the sole trigger and evaluates every vulnerability against four binary variables, derived from the SSVC decision framework (CMU CERT/CC and CISA):

Asset Exposure: Is the asset reachable by untrusted entities over a public network?

KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog?

Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation?

Technical Impact: Does successful exploitation grant Total control (arbitrary code execution, full/admin privileges) or only Partial control (limited access, information exposure, denial of service)?

Asset exposure is the highest-leverage variable. If you remove an asset from public reach, you flip the exposure variable from Yes to No, and the required timeline relaxes accordingly. Rapid7 Labs data underscores why exposure dominates: half of the vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild in Q1 2026 were zero-click, network-facing issues requiring no authentication, and by Q2 2026 nearly two-thirds required no user interaction at all. Attackers are going straight at exposed, unauthenticated surfaces.

CISA's new remediation tiers

The four variables combine into a graduated timeline (CISA BOD 26-04, Appendix A, Table 1). The tiers, simplified:

Tier

Timeline

Core criteria

1 (Critical)

3 days + forensic triage

On KEV and Total control

2 (High)

3 days (no triage)

Publicly exposed + Automatable + Total control, not yet on KEV

3 (Accelerated)

14 days

KEV-listed without Total control; or exposed + Partial control

4 (Standard)

60 days

Internal, automatable, Partial control

5 (Deferred)

Fix on next system upgrade

Internal + not KEV + not automatable + Partial control

Note that these timelines are dynamic. If a dormant vulnerability is added to the KEV, its clock can compress from 60 days to 3 overnight. Conversely, if you isolate an exposed asset, its clock relaxes. CISA explicitly counts isolation, mitigation, and uninstalling the vulnerable software as valid remediation; as such, a compensating control is a legitimate, compliant way to buy time for a safe patch.

The forensic triage mandate

This is the first of the requirements to have no precedent in earlier directives. For Tier 1 vulnerabilities (KEV + Total control), you must not only patch within three days, but run a concurrent forensic investigation to determine whether the asset is already compromised. Why? When an attacker exploits an exposed edge device, they establish persistence within hours; thus, patching three days later closes the door with the intruder already inside.

CISA's implementation guidance lays out a six-step, 72-hour protocol:

Phase

Window

What happens

1. Scoping

0–2 hrs

Identify in-scope devices; activate response team; open out-of-band comms

2. Preserve evidence

2–24 hrs

Capture volatile data (RAM, cache, registries) before any change

3. Patch & stabilize

2–24 hrs

Apply patches only after evidence is collected

4. Contain

6–24 hrs

Isolate infrastructure without tipping off the attacker

5. Triage analysis

24–48 hrs

Hunt IOCs; look for lateral movement and data staging

6. Escalation decision

48–72 hrs

Formal report; if compromised, report to CISA and pivot to full IR

Note the built-in tension between Step 2 and Step 3: patching reboots systems and overwrites the exact volatile memory that proves or disproves a compromise. You have to capture forensic evidence before you patch — at speed, across every affected endpoint. Doing that manually inside 72 hours is not always realistic.

Who CISA's BOD 26-04 applies to

BOD 26-04 is compulsory for all Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies. It excludes national security systems and DoD/Intelligence Community systems.

It reaches the private sector indirectly, but firmly. Agencies must review contracts and push compliance onto supply-chain partners. For FedRAMP and cloud offerings, agencies stay responsible for their hosted systems' compliance, which forces CSPs handling federal data to adopt the same 3-day triage standard. If you're a contractor or CSP touching federal data, treat this as your standard too.

Mapping Rapid7 to the directive

Meeting a 3-day clock with mandatory forensics is impossible through manual process. Here's how the Rapid7 Command Platform maps to each requirement.

Variable 1 (Exposure) → Surface Command

You can't calculate a timeline if you don't know what's exposed. Surface Command combines Cyber Asset Attack Surface Management (CAASM) with External Attack Surface Management (EASM), correlating continuous external scanning against an internal asset inventory ingested from your existing tools. The result is a single view of your true external attack surface — including the shadow IT attackers can see but your team can't. When it flags an exposed asset carrying a KEV-listed CVE, you can sever exposure to flip Variable 1 and de-escalate the timeline while you test the patch.

Variables 2 & 3 (KEV + Automation) → InsightVM and Active Risk

InsightVM tracks the KEV Catalog natively in its Threat Feed Dashboard, continuously updating which assets carry actively targeted vulnerabilities. Its Active Risk score — a 0–1,000 scale — moves beyond static CVSS by ingesting exploit intelligence from Metasploit, ExploitDB, the CISA KEV list, and Rapid7 Labs research. That mirrors the directive's own logic: a CVSS 7.5 bug with a weaponized Metasploit module will outrank a CVSS 9.8 bug with no known exploit — exactly the prioritization BOD 26-04 demands.

The NVD scoring gap → Exposure Command AI CVSS

The National Vulnerability Database can't keep pace with disclosure volume, leaving many CVEs unscored — a blind spot when a zero-day drops and you need a timeline immediately. Exposure Command fills it with an AI model trained on historical NVD data. On its own the model returns the correct severity classification 76% of the time; combined with Active Risk, that rises to 87%, with any miss never more than one classification off. Exposure Command also enriches every asset with business criticality and threat telemetry, and its Remediation Hub surfaces the fixes that cut the most risk.

The forensic mandate → Velociraptor

Velociraptor — the open-source DFIR project Rapid7 acquired in April 2021 — is built for exactly the scale and speed the triage mandate requires. It maps directly to the protocol: agents capture volatile memory and running-process data across thousands of endpoints simultaneously (Step 2), and analysts use Velociraptor Query Language to hunt CISA-provided IOCs enterprise-wide in real time, returning only relevant artifacts instead of pulling full disk images over the network (Step 5). That lets you satisfy the evidentiary requirement without delaying the Step 3 patch.

From severity to dollars

BOD 26-04 shares a core idea with modern risk management: technical severity isn't business impact. A high CVSS score doesn't answer the board's question of "how likely is this to cost us?"

The FAIR framework closes that gap by expressing risk as expected annual loss: Annualized Loss Expectancy = Loss Event Frequency × Loss Magnitude

BOD 26-04 is effectively a mechanism for pinning down Loss Event Frequency: by isolating vulnerabilities that are exploited (KEV), reachable (exposure), and scalable (automation), it identifies the ones statistically most likely to become a loss event. Feed Active Risk into the frequency side and FAIR into the cost side, and you can brief leadership in the language of capital, not CVE IDs.

Rapid7 case studies in the wild

Recent discoveries from Rapid7 Intelligence show the top tier in action:

Vulnerability

Impact

Why it's Tier 1

Rapid7 action

Microsoft SharePoint (CVE-2026-55040 + CVE-2026-63520)

Chained, the two flaws yield unauthenticated RCE via JWT bypass, running commands as the SharePoint service account

Internet-facing + total control (via the chain) + added to KEV after in-the-wild exploitation

Authenticated checks shipped to InsightVM/Exposure Command customers; Active Risk escalated to trigger triage

Palo Alto PAN-OS (CVE-2026-0300)

Unauthenticated buffer overflow in the User-ID Auth Portal; arbitrary code execution as root (CVSSv4 9.3)

Firewalls are exposed by definition; total impact; added to KEV May 6, 2026

Threat Feed integrated KEV status instantly; Velociraptor captured volatile RAM ahead of the patch

N-able N-central (CVE-2026-18577 + CVE-2026-18556)

Authentication bypass enabling full takeover of remote-management endpoints

High-value management assets; total control; added to KEV August 2026

Checks shipped via content release; Velociraptor hunted endpoint artifacts to satisfy triage

What's next for federal agencies and contractors?

If you're an FCEB agency or a contractor or CSP handling federal data, the following three moves matter most:

Get exposure right. Everything downstream depends on knowing what's publicly reachable. Establish continuous external-plus-internal asset visibility now.

Wire KEV into prioritization, not a spreadsheet. The clock starts the moment CISA updates the catalog. Ingestion has to be automated and continuous.

Pre-stage forensics. Decide today how you'll capture volatile evidence across endpoints inside 72 hours. If that's a manual runbook, it will fail under a real Tier 1 event.

CISA BOD 26-04's bottom line

BOD 26-04 retires "patch everything" in favor of operational precision: remediate the actively exploited, exposed, high-impact vulnerabilities in 72 hours, prove whether you've already been breached, and defer the rest. Meeting it takes continuous asset discovery, live threat intelligence, context-aware prioritization, and forensics at scale — which is precisely the shape of the Rapid7 Platform. For federal agencies it's a mandate; for everyone else, it's the clearest blueprint yet for risk-based vulnerability management.

Overview

On October 29, 2026, Ivanti updated its security advisory for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to include two additional vulnerabilities and released fixes for both. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3.1 score of 8.8; it allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate privileges. CVE-2026-118527, classified as generation of predictable numbers or identifiers (CWE-340), has an Ivanti-assigned CVSSv3.0 score of 4.3 and, according to CISA's KEV entry, allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.

Per Ivanti, exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers when these flaws are chained with CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). Rapid7 covered the original disclosure on October 13, 2026, when a fix for CVE-2026-104935 was available but the privilege escalation component remained unpatched. Fixes are now available for all three vulnerabilities.

On October 30, 2026, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation.

Title: Rapid7 Analysis: Unauthenticated File Upload to RCE in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764)
Context: Overview An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user
Full Text:
Overview

An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user. The entry point is the public customer connection used to start a support session. No account credentials or user interaction are required.

The flaw sits between the internal message router, brain, and an appliance-side customer worker, thin-scc. An attacker can put a reserved local router ID into a message's source address. The router forwards the message, and the worker accepts that address as proof that the request came from a local component. This gives the attacker access to an internal file-transfer service, including its native filesystem provider.

We first confirmed the file write then used the primitive to upload a PHP file to the site's public directory. Requesting that file gave us code execution as the site user. A Metasploit module now implements the chain with PHP and Unix Command targets.

We tested Remote Support 24.1.2, build 1524046, revision 4208-ddcf90715106aa0c0e19c103f8d2c412af4beff3. The test appliance had public issue-menu session starts and thin chat enabled (default). Other affected releases and fixed builds have not been established. The VM's base appliance version of Secure Remote Access, 7.1.0, is separate from the Remote Support application version.

Impact

The attacker controls both the contents of an uploaded file and its destination path, subject to the worker's filesystem permissions. The same origin forgery also reaches the file-send operation. We used it to retrieve /proc/self/environ to determine the base installation path of the Remote Support before dropping the payload

On the tested appliance, the native file service could write into the PHP document root. The Metasploit module returns code execution in the context of msfuser, UID 1000, which establishes unauthenticated remote code execution as the site user.

Technical Analysis

We will demonstrate how an attacker can start an anonymous session and then forge a message that the appliance will accept as local. Then outline how we can reach the native file transfer service, choose the uploaded file’s contents and destination and turn the file write into PHP execution.

Addresses use Ghidra image base 0x100000. Subtract that value for the raw ELF virtual address. Function names beginning with FUN_ are Ghidra labels; descriptive names are taken from diagnostic strings where available.

Starting an anonymous customer session

We begin by obtaining two customer keys from POST /api/start_session. These are fresh public guest sessions. The keys let the client use the customer transport, but do not identify a logged-in account. Each guest connects through the /nw WebSocket endpoint, using either the native or thin customer protocol.

source/app/write_app_chooser_config:

echo "ingredi support desk customer:|$BG_app_root/data/tmp/brain.sock" # [A1] echo "ingredi support desk customer thin:$BG_app_root/app/thin-scc-wrapper" # [A2]

app/write_app_chooser_config shows where the two customer protocols go. The native protocol reaches the brain socket at [A1]; the thin protocol launches a wrapper at [A2].

source/app/thin-scc-wrapper:

# ... omitted: protocol parsing and the alternative debug-site branch ... quoted=$(export PHPRC="$BG_app_root/config/php-cli.ini"; echo $gskey | $ingrediRoot/app/dbquote) if [[ $(echo "SELECT COUNT(1) FROM gw_sessions WHERE session_key = $quoted AND session_type = 'sdcust' AND (expiration IS NULL OR expiration>NOW())" | $db) != "1" ]]; then # [A3] echo "1 failure" >&0 exit 0 fi # ... omitted: reconnect throttling, customer-name setup, and settings generation ...

app/thin-scc-wrapper checks that the thin customer's key belongs to an unexpired sdcust session at [A3]. A key obtained through the public session-start endpoint passes this check.

app/thin-scc-wrapper, after the session check:

echo "0 success" >&0 workDir=`handleThinMint "$thinMint"` || exit if [[ ! -f "$workDir/thin-scc" ]]; then pushd "$workDir" cp $ingrediRoot/app/thin-scc . # ... omitted: license, image, and settings.ini setup ... else pushd "$workDir" fi export BRAIN_MELD_SOCKET_PATH=$ingrediRoot/data/tmp/brain.sock # ... omitted: server-side environment initialization ... ./thin-scc # [A4] Starts the worker inside the appliance environment. exitStatus=$?

The same wrapper then prepares a working directory and starts thin-scc at [A4]. This process runs on the appliance, even though it is handling an anonymous customer's thin session.

The native connection gives us a client for the internal message-routing system, referred to here as MRS. The thin connection gives us an appliance-side worker to address. Neither step requires a representative to accept the session.

A network message can claim to be local

MRS addresses have three parts: node:router:handler. Each message carries source and destination addresses in a 36-byte header made up of nine little-endian 32-bit fields.

Value used by the exploit

Source node

The customer's normal node

Source router

Changed to the reserved value 1

0x0c

Destination node

The worker's node

0x10

Destination router

The worker's router

0x14

Destination handler

Main dispatcher, 2048, on the tested build

0x24

Payload

Exploit

The Metasploit module carries out the chain using two fresh public customer sessions. It discovers the thin worker through Director.GetGatewaySessionValues for its own thin guest, sends the forged LocalFileTransfer request to the worker's main dispatcher, and serves the PHP bytes over its existing MRS connection. A separate upload server is not needed.

The module writes a random PHP filename into the site's public directory, then POSTs an execution token to the extensionless URL. The PHP file checks that token and unlinks itself before executing the payload. Target 0 runs a PHP payload; target 1 wraps a Unix command in PHP.

The aggregated logs are under $BG_app_root/log/. While a worker is running, its own logs are under $BG_app_root/data/tmp/sdcust_thin_client/<thinMint>/. The wrapper appends those logs to the site's log directory when the worker exits, then clears the per-worker copies. Collect both locations when investigating a live session.

The captured brain.ini and thin-scc.ini both had the debug output disabled with enabled=0. No debug log was captured, and we did not change the logging configuration. Brain's debug configuration also limits MRS_* categories to Info, so enabling its debug output alone would not guarantee detailed message payloads.

Names such as UploadFileStarted and DownloadFileEnded occur in the native protocol's callback code, but we did not find them in the collected logs. They should not be presented as default audit events

An introduction to CISA’s BOD 22-01

Issued nearly four years ago, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Binding Operational Directive 22-01 (BOD 22-01) has been adopted across both public and private sector organizations as a framework to ensure timely remediation of vulnerabilities being exploited by adversaries. By establishing a catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and emphasizing a risk-based, prioritized approach, it provides a clear model for organizations to strengthen their cybersecurity posture and reduce exposure to real-world threats.

InsightGovCloud, Rapid7’s FedRAMP-authorized suite of security solutions, helps organizations implement BOD 22-01 by providing automated vulnerability scanning, real-time alerts for KEVs, and reporting aligned with regulatory requirements. Public and private sector teams can quickly identify at-risk assets, prioritize remediation efforts based on active exploitation, and maintain an auditable record of compliance. By leveraging our secure, cloud-based platform, organizations gain continuous visibility, streamlined vulnerability management, and the confidence that remediation aligns with federal cybersecurity standards.

Title: Simplify User Access Management with SCIM on Rapid7 Command Platform
Context: Keep user information current: Synchronize supported user attributes as information changes
Full Text:
Managing access to security tools shouldn't require another manual process. As organizations grow, keeping user accounts and permissions up to date becomes increasingly complex. Employees join, change roles, and leave, creating a constant need to update access across applications.

When these processes rely on manual administration, delays and oversights can introduce unnecessary work and security risk.

Rapid7 Command Platform now supports System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM), enabling customers to automate user provisioning and deprovisioning through their existing identity provider (IdP).

This helps organizations reduce administrative overhead, maintain more consistent access controls, and manage identity at scale.

Automate user access throughout the employee lifecycle

SCIM is an open standard that enables identity providers, such as Okta, to automatically manage user accounts in connected applications.

With SCIM enabled, Rapid7 Command Platform customers can:

Automate provisioning: Create accounts when employees join or need access.

Keep user information current: Synchronize supported user attributes as information changes.

Simplify offboarding: Automatically deactivate accounts when users no longer require access.

Manage groups at scale: Synchronize group membership to help streamline access administration.

Rather than manually updating accounts in Command Platform, administrators can manage supported identity lifecycle changes through their existing IdP.

Less administration, more consistent access control

Consider a common scenario: An employee leaves the organization. Without automated provisioning, an administrator must remember to deactivate that employee's access across their applications. If an account is missed, it could remain active longer than intended.

With SCIM, changes made in the organization's identity provider can automatically trigger corresponding account updates in Command Platform.

By introducing SCIM at the platform level, Rapid7 helps organizations:

Reduce operational overhead by eliminating repetitive account-management tasks.

Strengthen access governance by reducing stale accounts and keeping user information aligned with identity provider policies.

Scale more efficiently by centralizing identity lifecycle management for supported Command Platform applications.

For organizations with security and compliance requirements, these capabilities also help support consistent onboarding and offboarding processes.

Get started with SCIM

Platform administrators can configure SCIM through Command Platform's SSO settings using their existing identity provider. SCIM is disabled by default and requires configuration before automated provisioning begins.

Title: CVE-2026-111497: Critical out-of-bounds write in the Node.js Brotli decoder
Context: Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497...
Full Text:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js Project published a security advisory for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The vulnerability affects the Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x release lines. Node.js rates the issue High, while Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), gives it a critical CVSSv4 score of 9.2.

An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory. According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder.

On October 27, 2026, CVE-2026-111497 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. Given the vulnerability's potential to disclose memory or enable remote code execution (RCE), Rapid7 recommends that organizations prioritize remediation.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-111497 is classified as an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and an unchecked return value (CWE-252). Per the vendor advisory, the decoder handled an invalid Brotli block switch as a temporary need for more input instead of a permanent format error. The streaming decoder then continued appending input bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, allowing malformed input to write beyond the buffer and corrupt process memory.

The vulnerability originates in Google Brotli, which the affected Node.js release lines bundle as a dependency. The CVE record identifies affected upstream Brotli ranges on all platforms as versions 1.0.3 before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1, and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1. The Node.js Project remediated its bundled decoder in the fixed Node.js releases listed below.

Because CVE-2026-111497 affects the upstream Google Brotli decoder, its reach is not limited to Node.js. Vendor and project advisories have also identified affected implementations in Bun, Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, .NET, Envoy and Istio, brotli4j, and operating-system packages. Affected versions, default exposure, and remediation vary by product; the presence of an affected decoder does not by itself establish exposure unless an application processes attacker-controlled Brotli data. Organizations should consult the relevant downstream vendor or distribution advisories to identify affected versions, assess exposure, and determine appropriate remediation.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor-supplied security updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-111497. Organizations running an affected Node.js release should upgrade on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles:

Node.js 22.x releases before 22.23.4 are affected; upgrade to 22.23.4 or later.

Node.js 24.x releases before 24.22.1 are affected; upgrade to 24.22.1 or later.

Node.js 26.x releases before 26.12.1 are affected; upgrade to 26.12.1 or later.

The vendor states that end-of-life Node.js release lines should also be treated as affected when a security release occurs. Organizations using an end-of-life release should migrate to a supported, fixed release line. Node.js has not published a vendor-supported workaround; if an immediate upgrade is not possible, Rapid7 recommends restricting or disabling application paths that decompress untrusted Brotli data as a temporary exposure-reduction measure.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the Node.js security advisory.

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497 with an authenticated vulnerability check for Linux, macOS, and Windows, available in the October 26 content release.

October 26, 2026: Updated the Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose section to reflect coverage availability.

Title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in PHP
Context: Overview On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP
Full Text:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges.

CVE

CVSSv4

Description

CVE-2026-109618

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via OOM corruption

CVE-2026-109619

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via stale global state

All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs.

The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon.

Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles.

Multiple public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are now available. Rapid7 researchers have reviewed these and observe that each demonstrates RCE only against a specific combination of operating system, PHP version, and web server, and none appears to be broadly reliable. Rapid7’s own research supports this. Our attempts so far have produced a working exploit only under narrow lab conditions, and exploitation depends on assumptions that are unlikely to hold on internet-facing instances. We are continuing to investigate approaches that could improve portability, but have not yet developed a reliable, general-purpose exploit. Rapid7 has not observed exploitation in the wild, though there are multiple reports of exploitation attempts, which is expected for a vulnerability of this profile. The situation is evolving quickly, and a more portable exploit technique could emerge at any time. The current difficulty of reliable exploitation should be treated as a window to patch rather than a reason to delay, and Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis.

Update #1: On October 26, 2026, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. CISA set the remediation due date to October 29, 2026, for affected Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies and directs them to follow the associated BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements. Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis and investigating for prior compromise.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-109618: Memory corruption during OOM handling

According to the OOM advisory, PHP can abruptly abandon request processing when a memory allocation fails. If internal request data is only partly initialized, that exit can leave invalid data for request cleanup to use. Crafted multipart requests, used for forms and file uploads, can exhaust memory even when their size appears to meet PHP's configured limits. Application operations that allocate memory in response to attacker input can also trigger OOM.

Apache mod_php runs cleanup even when request startup fails, enabling the demonstrated attack before application code executes. The advisory reports RCE over HTTP with default PHP input and memory limits, including multi-worker prefork deployments. PHP-FPM terminates a worker when startup fails, preventing that particular sequence. Source analysis supports FPM susceptibility after successful startup, but the advisory reports no complete FPM exploit for this CVE. Exploit portability and reliability depend on the PHP build, extensions, frontend behavior, and memory layout.

CVE-2026-109619: Use after free across requests

PHP can reuse a worker process to handle multiple HTTP requests. The stale-state advisory describes internal state that still points to memory freed at the end of an earlier request. A later request handled by the same worker can access that stale value before normal initialization clears it. Fatal errors, including memory exhaustion and execution timeouts, can interrupt state cleanup; some nonfatal diagnostics during shutdown can also repopulate error state after it was reset.

The advisory confirms RCE against mod_php through PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace feature, when fatal_error_backtraces is enabled (the default), where a later initialization diagnostic accesses stale backtrace state. It also confirms session lifecycle RCE against mod_php and FPM. Session upload progress, PHP's upload-tracking feature, is enabled by default and can act as an early consumer of stale session or decoder state before normal initialization; reaching this consumer does not itself require an application call to session_start().

The validated FPM session path requires a suitable application operation to leave state behind after successful startup, followed by a fatal error and another request that consumes the stale state through session upload progress. Both requests must reach the same worker. Multiple workers and worker recycling can reduce success per request, but do not eliminate the condition.

Mitigation guidance

PHP has released fixes for both vulnerabilities. Organizations should prioritize updating to the appropriate fixed release or a vendor package containing both complete patches. The PHP advisories list these affected and fixed versions:

PHP 8.2 releases before 8.2.35: Update to 8.2.35

PHP 8.3 releases before 8.3.36: Update to 8.3.36

PHP 8.4 releases before 8.4.27: Update to 8.4.27

PHP 8.5 releases before 8.5.12: Update to 8.5.12

Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance; check your vendor for updated packages. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine upstream updates. For this incident, PHP has supplied limited source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Organizations running older branches should obtain a vendor fix, use the source backports described in the PHP announcement, or upgrade to a supported version. PHP also warns that rpms.remirepo.net will not have updates on October 21, 2026, and urges its users to switch to distribution packages or build from source.

Note that an update containing both complete fixes is the only complete remediation.

PHP's temporary configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and require careful deployment:

For the OOM issue, enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through FPM pool or Apache configuration that applications cannot override. This disables PHP's per-request memory cap and removes the predictable PHP-limit failure used by the confirmed exploit. An underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Restart every worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit.

For the session lifecycle path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing, then restart every worker. Application-level ini_set() and FPM .user.ini are too late. This addresses the confirmed session paths only.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This addresses the confirmed fatal backtrace path only; other retained state remains a concern.

Disabling PHP's memory cap makes independent resource controls particularly important. PHP recommends post_max_size=8M where uploads are unnecessary or post_max_size=32M where they are needed, with upload_max_filesize below that limit. At the frontend, bound decoded request size, input and multipart counts, headers per part, and nesting depth, including requests without a usable Content-Length. If the application does not use multipart data, block those requests before they reach PHP.

Container or cgroup memory limits are also incomplete: allocation failures remain possible, and enforcement can kill the master process and all workers unless workers are isolated. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable allocation-failure path.

For stale-state exposure, correct invalid or deprecated per-request settings and attacker-reachable fatal errors or timeouts. Hiding diagnostics through error_reporting, display_errors, log_errors, or @ does not prevent stale-state access. The absence of relevant log entries is not proof that an installation is safe.

For the latest mitigation guidance, refer to PHP's OOM corruption advisory and stale global state advisory.

Rapid7 customers

To learn how to use Rapid7 capabilities to find systems affected by these vulnerabilities and for answers to common questions, read the PHP2Shell documentation.

For Rapid7 Customers with questions regarding Rapid7 products and their usage of PHP please consult this page.

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with remote unauthenticated vulnerability checks, available in a dedicated release that followed the regular October 21 content release.

Rapid7 has also released authenticated scan checks for both the Scan Engine and the Agent for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as part of the October 22 content release.

Authenticated, package-based checks are now available for a variety of Linux distributions. These checks evaluate installed distribution packages, so they can recognize backported fixes that keep the original upstream PHP version number. Run an authenticated scan with this content release to use them. For the full list of checks and supported distribution versions, read Rapid7’s PHP2Shell documentation, where package-based coverage for other distributions will be added as their fixes are published.

In a dedicated October 23 content release following the regular release, Rapid7 has released coverage for CVE-2026-115560, published on October 23 by the PHP Foundation. A mitigation technique is available, but no patch has yet been published. Exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 relies on non-standard configuration.

Current scope for authenticated coverage: Windows, macOS and Linux. Remote unauthenticated coverage provides coverage regardless of web-server OS.

Velociraptor

A Velociraptor Artifact Generic.Applications.PHPInventory is available to inventory PHP installations on Windows, Linux and macOS for remediation scoping. This artifact allows for the collection of package versions, common binary and module paths, and running PHP processes.

Title: Q3 2026 Threat Update: Attackers Are Exploiting Vulnerabilities Within 3 Days
Context: Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction Q3's vulnerability data reveals another concerning pattern: Of the 43 newly exploited high- and critical-...
Full Text:
Three days is the average time between a high-severity vulnerability becoming public and its exploitation, according to the latest Quarterly Threat Landscape Report from Rapid7. And 71% of the exploitation tracked in Q3 occurred within the first seven days.

For security teams already managing growing vulnerability backlogs, this creates a difficult question: How do you reduce exposure when attackers can exploit vulnerabilities before your next patching window?

Rapid7's Q3 2026 research brings together vulnerability intelligence, ransomware activity, APT tracking, and underground forum intelligence to show where attacker activity is concentrated.

The exploitation window has narrowed, big time

Rapid7 tracked 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities this quarter, down 7% from Q2 but still 19% higher than the same period last year.

The number of newly exploited vulnerabilities isn't growing at the same rate as disclosures. The more pressing concern is how quickly attackers exploit the vulnerabilities they choose. On average, exploitation occurred just three days after public disclosure. The report also found that 80% of tracked exploitation occurred within 14 days and 90% within 30 days.

That timeline creates a serious challenge for organizations relying on fixed remediation schedules. It also reinforces the need to distinguish between vulnerabilities that are theoretically severe and those that pose an immediate, exploitable risk.

The report examines the exploitation timeline in greater detail, including the vulnerability characteristics that make certain exposures particularly attractive to attackers.

Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction

Q3's vulnerability data reveals another concerning pattern: Of the 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities tracked, 34 (79%) required no authentication or user interaction.

This provides attackers a potential path into exposed systems, no stolen credentials or malicious content interaction necessary. An internet-facing service with an exploitable vulnerability may require immediate attention, particularly when an attacker can reach it without authenticating.

This makes attack surface visibility and contextual prioritization essential. Security teams need to understand which systems are externally accessible, which vulnerabilities are actively exploited, and whether existing controls can prevent or limit compromise.

A CVSS score alone won’t give you the answers. The report explores the characteristics of exploited vulnerabilities and why understanding reachability is critical to reducing risk.

AI is taking on a more operational role in attacks

In Q3, 8% of the threat reporting tracked by Rapid7 cited AI as an operational component. The research identifies a shift from using AI primarily to help draft content or code toward supporting tactical decisions and execution within attack campaigns.

In the documented cases, human operators continued to select targets and determine objectives, but relied on AI assistance for technique selection, target assessment, and adapting when an attack step failed.

The report also examines how threat actors split malicious objectives across multiple AI sessions to evade provider safeguards. There are serious implications for detection in these findings. AI-enabled attacks also reinforce the value of monitoring and quickly adapting to attacker behavior rather than relying exclusively on known malware signatures or threat actor identities.

The report provides additional context on how AI appeared in tracked campaigns and what defenders should monitor.

The next step: Prioritize exposure before attackers exploit it

Q3's findings reveal a challenge that vulnerability counts alone can’t explain. Attackers exploited 43 newly tracked vulnerabilities this quarter, yet the average exploitation window was just three days. Meanwhile, underground forum monitoring identified 41 posts advertising RDP or network access, demonstrating continued interest in selling access to compromised environments.

Security teams must account for both the vulnerabilities attackers can exploit directly and the access they can obtain through other means.

Start by identifying externally accessible assets and the vulnerabilities affecting them. Prioritize known exploitation, unauthenticated access paths, and systems supporting critical business functions. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, assess compensating controls and detection coverage.
